text: Bartolomé Esteban Murillo is best known for his religious works, but he also painted many contemporary women and children, such as flower girls, street urchins and beggars. Those lively, realistic pictures form an extensive record of everyday life in his time. He painted two self-portraits, one now in the Frick Collection and one in London's National Gallery, made about twenty years apart. The two museums held an exhibition of them in 2017. He was probably born in December 1617 to a barber surgeon.

Eastman Johnson co-founded the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and his name is inscribed at its entrance. He was best known for genre paintings of everyday scenes and for portraits of both ordinary people and prominent Americans such as Abraham Lincoln, Nathaniel Hawthorne and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. His later works often show the influence of the 17th-century Dutch masters, whom he studied in The Hague in the 1850s. In his day he was known as the American Rembrandt.

Gustave De Smet was one of the founders of Flemish Expressionism, together with Constant Permeke and Frits Van den Berghe. Before World War I these artists belonged to the second group of the Latem School, a loose group working in the rural Lys river area around Sint-Martens-Latem, south of Ghent. They aimed to renew Belgian art by turning away from bourgeois art. Some of their works relate to German expressionism through distorted forms and dynamic compositions, while others show cubist elements. De Smet was a Belgian painter and printmaker.

Alfred Choubrac and Jules Chéret are considered pioneers of the modern coloured and illustrated poster of the Belle Époque. Choubrac was born in Montmartre, and with his elder brother Léon he trained as a classical artist at the École des Beaux Arts under Charles Doërr and Isidore Pils. The brothers began making posters very early in their careers. From 1875 they combined modern colour and typographic techniques with graphics, using chromolithography. Alfred also worked as a painter, illustrator and costume designer.

Jan Mankes died of tuberculosis at the age of 30 after producing around 200 paintings, 100 drawings and 50 prints. His restrained, detailed work ranged from self-portraits to landscapes and studies of birds and animals. He had a reputation as an ascetic who lived in self-chosen isolation in De Knipe, Friesland, far from the centre of the country's culture. In reality he read the leading newspapers and magazines, and friends supplied him with clippings. He had also lived in The Hague and, because of his tuberculosis, in Eerbeek.

Jan Toorop worked in several styles, including Symbolism, Art Nouveau and Pointillism, and his early work was influenced by Amsterdam Impressionism. He was born in Purworejo on Java in the Dutch East Indies, the third of five children, and lived on the island of Bangka near Sumatra until he was nine. Then he was sent to school in Batavia. In 1869 he left Indonesia for the Netherlands, where he studied in Delft and Amsterdam. In 1880 he became a student at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam.

Edward Duncan was apprenticed to Robert Havell, the principal aquatint engraver of Audubon's Birds of America. That gave him frequent opportunities to study the work of Havell's brother, the watercolourist William Havell, and it developed his taste for drawing and colour. After training under the Havell brothers, he started his own engraving studio and mainly made prints. He was known for coastal views and shipping. He was a member of the Royal Watercolour Society and received royal patronage from Queen Victoria.

Jacobus Cornelis Gaal came from a family of painters and etchers, and his father Pieter taught him. He focused on portraits and miniatures, including one of his father. Some of his paintings were shown in exhibitions in Middelburg in 1822, in Amsterdam in 1852 and in The Hague in 1853. He painted portraits of King William I and King William II. During his life he made several trips down the Rhine. He was born in Oost-Souburg and died in Kampen.

Emile Claus was the twelfth child in a family of thirteen, born in Sint-Eloois-Vijve, a village on the banks of the river Lys. His father was a grocer-publican and for some time a town councillor. As a child he already loved drawing, and on Sundays he walked three kilometres to the Academy of Waregem to learn to draw. He graduated from the academy with a gold medal. His father allowed him to take drawing classes but did not fancy an artist's career for his son.

Julian Fałat studied at the Kraków School of Fine Arts under Władysław Łuszczkiewicz, then at the Art Academy of Munich. On his travels around Europe and Asia he compiled studies that helped develop his art. Typical themes in his painting are Polish landscapes, hunting scenes, portraits and travel observations. He accepted an invitation from the future German Emperor Wilhelm II to work as court painter in Berlin and stayed there from 1886 to 1895. In 1895 he became director of the Kraków School of Fine Arts.

Jules De Bruycker is considered one of the foremost Belgian graphic artists after James Ensor, and he reached a high level of technical virtuosity. He is best known for his scenes of his home town Ghent, his architectural views of cathedrals, his war prints and his book illustrations. His family ran a small upholstery and wallpapering business in Ghent. Showing precocious talent, he enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts there at ten. When his father died four years later, he stopped attending classes and joined the family business, but he kept honing his skills without formal training.

Frans Hals lived and worked in Haarlem, where the authorities frowned on religious painting in places of worship but citizens liked to decorate their homes with works of art. Wealthy burghers sought him out for portraits of individuals, married couples, families and institutional groups. He also painted tronies for the general market. There were two quite distinct schools of portraiture in 17th-century Haarlem, a neat one represented by Verspronck and a looser, more painterly style at which Hals excelled. Some of his portraits have a subdued palette that reflects the serious tones of his clients' wardrobes.

Augustin de Saint-Aubin belonged to an important dynasty of French designers and engravers. He was born in Paris to the king's embroiderer, Gabriel Germain de Saint-Aubin. His six siblings included the brothers Charles-Germain and Gabriel-Jacques, and together they were known as the Book of Saint-Aubin. His niece Marie-François was an artist too. Trained by his brother, he later studied with Étienne Fessard, Nicolas-Henry Tardieu and Laurent Cars.

John Trumbull is best known for historical paintings of the American Revolutionary War, in which he served. He has been called the Painter of the Revolution. His Declaration of Independence, one of four of his paintings in the rotunda of the United States Capitol, appears on the reverse of the current two-dollar bill. He was born in Lebanon, Connecticut, the son of Jonathan Trumbull, who served as governor of Connecticut from 1769 to 1784. Both sides of his family descended from early Puritan settlers of Connecticut.

Józef Ignacy Kraszewski wrote over 200 novels and several hundred shorter works. He was born in Warsaw into a noble family and spent much of his youth with his maternal grandparents in Romanów. His literary career began in 1830. He was imprisoned for his involvement in the November Uprising but kept supporting Polish independence. He spent his later years in Dresden and died in Geneva. Besides writing, he was a historian, a publisher, a painter and a musician.

Christian Krohg was inspired by the realism movement and often chose motifs from everyday life. From 1909 to 1925 he was the director and first professor at the Norwegian Academy of Arts. He was born at Vestre Aker, now Oslo, a grandson of a government minister of the same name. His father was a civil servant, journalist and author. His mother died when he was only eight, and his father's sister took over the household and the upbringing of the children. He also worked as a journalist.

Caspar Wolf is known mostly for dramatic paintings of the Alps. Albrecht von Haller's poems on the Alps and the Sturm und Drang movement strongly influenced him. After 1773 he mostly painted glaciers and waterfalls. The son of a furniture maker, he trained in Konstanz and worked in Augsburg, Munich and Passau as a decoration painter, but he could not sell his work and went back disappointed to his home town. In 1769 he went to Paris and worked with Philip James de Loutherbourg. In 1774 he moved to Bern.

Friedrich Brentel's principal work is a set of plates for The Funeral of Charles III, Duke of Lorraine, and the royal entry of his son as the new duke, published at Nancy in 1611. They follow designs by Claude de La Ruelle and Jean La Hire and are etched in a slight, spirited manner. One plate, showing a single horse and rider, is thought to be the first etching by the Nancy court painter Jacques Bellange. Brentel was born in Lauingen and became a citizen of Strasbourg in 1601.

Barthel Beham was the younger brother of Hans Sebald Beham and was born into a family of artists in Nuremberg. He learned his art from his elder brother and from Albrecht Dürer, and he was particularly active as an engraver in the 1520s, creating tiny works of magnificent detail. He was also fascinated with antiquity and may have worked with Marcantonio Raimondi in Bologna and Rome. In 1525 he was banished from Lutheran Nuremberg, along with his brother and Georg Pencz, for asserting his disbelief in baptism, Christ and transubstantiation.

Edward William Cooke was raised among artists. His father, George Cooke, was a well-known line engraver, and so was his uncle William Bernard Cooke. Edward was a precocious draughtsman and a skilled engraver from an early age, and he preferred marine subjects, especially sailing ships. At eighteen he published Shipping and Craft, a series of accomplished engravings, in 1829. He benefited from the advice of many of his father's associates, notably Clarkson Stanfield.

Edward Theodore Compton made about 300 major ascents as a mountaineer, including no fewer than 27 first ascents. He is well known for his paintings and drawings of alpine scenery. He was born in Stoke Newington in London, the son of an art-loving insurance agent, and grew up in a deeply religious Quaker household. He attended Sidcot School from 1861 to 1864 and various art schools, including for a time the Royal Academy in London, but he was mainly self-taught in art.

The Mantegna Tarocchi are two different sets of fifty 15th-century Italian engravings by two unknown artists. The sets are known as the E-series and the S-series Tarocchi, and their makers are called the Master of the E-series Tarocchi and the Master of the S-series Tarocchi. The name Mantegna appears to be a mistaken confusion by later writers. Despite the name, the prints are educational visual aids that show personifications of social classes and abstractions. There are also a number of copies and later versions.

Theodor Matham came from a family of engravers: his father Jacob Matham was the better known, and his brothers Jan and Adriaen were engravers too. Born in Haarlem in 1589, he went to Italy and studied under Cornelius Bloemaert. He then returned to Haarlem, where he engraved an important number of plates. He signed his plates with the letters TM and the word fecit or sculpsit.

Johannes Bosboom was known especially for his paintings of church interiors. He was born in The Hague, and at fourteen he became a student of Bartholomeus van Hove and painted in his studio with Van Hove's son Hubertus. Together they worked on pieces of scenery that Van Hove created for the Royal Theatre in The Hague. Bosboom also took lessons at the Hague Academy of Art over several years, where he met Anthonie Waldorp and Wijnand Nuyen. In 1851 he married the novelist Anna Louisa Geertruida Bosboom-Toussaint.

Cornelis Dusart trained with Adriaen van Ostade from about 1675 to 1679, and the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke accepted him in 1679. His works are similar in style and subject to those of his mentor. Especially notable are his highly finished drawings of peasants, shown singly in coloured chalks and watercolor. Born in Haarlem, he died there too. He worked as a Dutch genre painter and printmaker.

Abraham Blooteling produced a large number of etchings and some line engravings, and he also worked in mezzotint, a technique he is known to have adopted by 1671. He has sometimes been credited with inventing the rocker, a tool for preparing mezzotint plates, and with introducing the technique into England. He was born in Amsterdam and was probably a pupil of the Visschers. After the French incursions into the Netherlands in 1672 he went to England, where he had some success but stayed only two or three years.

Many historical paintings by Konstantin Makovsky, such as Beneath the Crown from 1889, also known as The Russian Bride's Attire, showed an idealized view of Russian life of earlier centuries. He was a Russian painter of the Belle Époque and belonged to the Wanderers. He is often considered a representative of Academic art. His father, Egor Makovsky, was an art figure and amateur painter.

Abraham Bloemaert was an important teacher who trained most of the Utrecht Caravaggisti. He initially worked in the style of the Haarlem Mannerists, but by the beginning of the 17th century he changed his style to suit the new Baroque. He mostly painted history subjects and some landscapes. He was born in Gorinchem, the son of the architect Cornelis Bloemaert I, who moved the family to Utrecht in 1575. There he was first a pupil of Gerrit Splinter and of Joos de Beer.

Franz Thonner made his first trip to the African interior in the spring of 1896 to explore the botany and people of the northern Congo Basin. Besides a comprehensive collection of plants, he embarked on a thorough ethnographic study of the region. He was an Austrian botanist from Vienna and a scientist of independent means who explored Europe and North Africa. In 1891, at age 28, he privately published a key to the families of flowering plants of the world.

Olga Boznańska's style was close to French Impressionism, though she rejected that label. She was born in Kraków, the daughter of Adam Nowina Boznański, from a noble Polish family who worked as a railway engineer, and the teacher Eugénie, née Mondan, who came from Valence in France. She learned drawing first from her mother, who taught at the convent school of the Premonstratensians in Imbramowice near Kraków. Then she studied with Józef Siedlecki, Kazimierz Pochwalski and Antoni Piotrowski.

Theo Nieuwenhuis is known as one of the best Dutch artists to work in the style called Nieuwe Kunst, or Art Nouveau. He applied it to many different media, from watercolour and lithography to woodcarving and ceramics. He was educated at the State Normal School for Applied Art and the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Amsterdam, where he was a pupil of John Roelof de Kruyff. He traveled extensively early in his career. He was based in Amsterdam from 1883 to 1888.

Wilhelm von Kobell was the son of the landscape painter Ferdinand Kobell, who cited Claude Lorrain as his influence. His first lessons came from his father and his uncle Franz Kobell. He received further training in engraving under Franz Anton von Leydendorf and Egid Verhelst at the drawing academy in Mannheim. He studied the works in the galleries of Mannheim and Düsseldorf. He copied Wouwerman especially. During this time he practiced various styles, including 17th-century Dutch painting and 18th-century English art.

Willem Jacobsz Delff learned painting from his father, Jacob Willemsz Delff the Elder, who painted a family portrait with his wife and sons. His brothers were artists in their own right: Cornelis became a still life painter, and Rochus became a portrait painter like their father. Willem married a daughter of Michiel Jansz van Mierevelt and became a well-known engraver. His son Jacob Willemsz Delff the Younger became a painter. Willem died on 14 April 1638.

Dominicus Custos worked in the service of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague. He was a Flemish artist, printer and copperplate engraver, born in Antwerp, the son of Pieter Balten. In Augsburg he became the second husband of the widow of the goldsmith Bartholomäus Kilian, and he trained her sons Wolfgang and Lukas Kilian in engraving after their father's death. His own son David Custodis was also an Augsburg engraver. With the humanist Marcus Henning he produced Tirolensium principum comitum, which appeared in 1599 and depicted 28 Counts of Tyrol.

Renold Elstracke was one of the earliest engravers in England. He was the son of Josephe Elstrage of Lukeland, in the province of Liège, who came to England in 1551. He was in all probability a pupil of Crispin van de Passe the Elder at Cologne, and he came to England at the same time as the younger members of the Van de Passe family. A print of Charles I is ascribed to Elstracke, which would mean he lived on into that king's reign. Nobody knows when he died. The latest mention of him is from 1625.

Gustave Moreau was an influential forerunner of symbolism in the visual arts in the 1860s, and at the height of the movement in the 1890s he was among its most significant painters. Jean Cassou called him the Symbolist painter par excellence. He was prolific and produced over 15,000 paintings, watercolors and drawings. Moreau painted allegories and the traditional biblical and mythological subjects favored by the fine art academies. The art historian Robert Delevoy wrote that Moreau brought symbolist polyvalence to its highest point in Jupiter and Semele.

Edward Mitchell Bannister won a first prize in painting at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition, which brought him national recognition. Born in colonial New Brunswick, he spent his adult life in New England. With his wife Christiana Carteaux he was a prominent member of African-American cultural and political communities, such as the Boston abolition movement. He painted in oils and belonged to the American Barbizon School. He was also a founding member of the Providence Art Club and the Rhode Island School of Design.

Jean-Baptiste Oudry is particularly well known for his naturalistic pictures of animals and his hunt pieces depicting game. He was born in Paris, the son of Jacques Oudry, a painter and art dealer, and Nicole Papillon. His father directed the Académie de Saint-Luc art school, which Oudry joined. At first he concentrated on portraiture, and he was a pupil and perhaps a collaborator of Nicolas de Largillière from 1707 to 1712. His son Jacques-Charles was also a painter.

John Warwick Smith was the son of a gardener to the Gilpin family, and that connection let him study art under the animal painter Sawrey Gilpin. He was born at Irthington near Carlisle and educated at St. Bees. He became known as a skilful topographical draughtsman and was employed on Samuel Middiman's Select Views in Great Britain. The patronage of George Greville, 2nd Earl of Warwick, enabled him to travel to Italy between 1776 and 1781. There he met other British artists such as Francis Towne and Thomas Hearne.

Andrea Mantegna was the son-in-law of Jacopo Bellini. Like other artists of the time, he experimented with perspective, for example by lowering the horizon to create a sense of greater monumentality. His flinty, metallic landscapes and somewhat stony figures show a fundamentally sculptural approach to painting. He also led a workshop that was the leading producer of prints in Venice before 1500. He was born in Isola di Carturo, close to Padua, the second son of a carpenter named Biagio.

Venny Soldan-Brofeldt belonged to the Swedish-speaking population of Finland. She was born Wendla Irene Soldan in Helsinki, and Swedish was spoken at home. Her father was the Director of the Mint of Finland and her mother, Marie Müller, was German. Her family wholeheartedly supported her desire to become an artist. From 1880 to 1884 she attended the drawing school of the Finnish Art Association, and she also studied privately with Maria Wiik. She worked as a painter, illustrator, graphic artist, wood sculptor and jewelry designer.

Shibata Zeshin has been called Japan's greatest lacquerer. Born and raised in Edo, he worked as a lacquer painter and print artist in the late Edo period and early Meiji era. His reputation as a painter and print artist is more complex. In Japan he is seen as both too modern, a panderer to the Westernization movement, and an overly conservative traditionalist who did nothing to stand out from his contemporaries. Despite that, he is well regarded and much studied in the West, in Britain and the United States in particular.

Antoon Derkinderen grew up in 's-Hertogenbosch, a deeply Catholic and conservative town, as the son of a gold- and silversmith. From 1874 to 1878 he went to the daytime school for primary school teachers there. The simple reason was that the education was solid and free of charge. He qualified to teach drawing. He worked as a painter, glass artist and designer of book covers.

At fifteen Théodore Chassériau painted a portrait of Prosper Marilhat that made him the youngest painter exhibited at the Louvre. He was a Dominican-born French Romantic painter noted for his portraits and for Orientalist images inspired by his travels to Algeria. Early in his career he painted in a Neoclassical style close to that of his teacher Ingres. In his later works Delacroix strongly influenced him. He was a prolific draftsman and made a suite of prints to illustrate Shakespeare's Othello.

Both of Robert Wilhelm Ekman's parents died when he was about ten, leaving five orphans who were placed with other families. His father had been a medical doctor and a mayor in Uusikaupunki, where Robert was born into an upper-class family. The children's schooling was incomplete, and there was no chance of higher academic education. Robert first studied art under the Finnish painter Gustaf Wilhelm Finnberg. He became a significant teacher and painter of Finnish romantic portraits and early national romanticism.

Gustave Caillebotte belonged to the Impressionists as both painter and patron, although he painted in a more realistic manner than many others in the group. He was known for his early interest in photography as an art form. Because of his family's wealth, he supported many of his fellow Impressionists. When he died, the collection of their works that he bequeathed became the central collection of Impressionism for the French Republic, despite considerable controversy. His most well known work is Paris Street, Rainy Day.

Jan de Beijer produced some 1500 drawings of towns and buildings in the present-day Netherlands, Belgium and Germany, and over 600 of them were reproduced as engravings by other artists. He travelled through the Netherlands in summer to draw views of cities and towns as well as castles. In winter he stayed at home to make colour drawings from his sketches in the field. He also made drawings that other artists could use to produce engravings. He was born in 1703.

William Henry Margetson is mainly known for his aesthetic portraits of women. He was born at Camberwell in London and studied at Dulwich College, and later at the Royal College of Art and the Royal Academy Schools. In 1885 he first exhibited at the Royal Academy, and later also at the Royal Society of British Artists and the Grosvenor Gallery. In late 1885 he won the Armitage Medal for his studies at the Academy, and the medal is now in the British Museum. He painted in oils and watercolours.

Diego Velázquez was the leading artist at the court of King Philip IV of Spain and of the Spanish Golden Age. He began to paint in a precise tenebrist style and later developed a freer manner with bold brushwork. Besides scenes of historical and cultural significance, he painted scores of portraits of the Spanish royal family and of commoners. He is generally considered one of the greatest artists in the history of Western art. He was baptised in June 1599 and died in August 1660.

Wojciech Gerson was one of the foremost representatives of the Polish school of Realism during the Partitions of Poland. He served for a long time as a professor at the School of Fine Arts in Warsaw, where he taught future leading figures of Polish neo-romanticism such as Józef Chełmoński and Leon Wyczółkowski. He also wrote art reviews and published a book of anatomy for artists. A large number of his paintings were stolen by Nazi Germany in World War II and never recovered.

Hiroshige II inherited his name after the death in 1858 of his master Hiroshige, whose daughter he married. In 1865 he moved from Edo to Yokohama after dissolving his marriage and began using the name Kisai Risshō. His work so resembles his master's that scholars have often confused them. He was born Suzuki Chinpei in 1826, and it is said he was the son of a fireman, as Hiroshige was. He was apprenticed to Hiroshige under the name Shigenobu.

Andreas Achenbach is considered one of the founders of the Düsseldorf School. He was a German landscape and seascape painter in the Romantic style. His brother Oswald was also a well-known landscape painter, and together, going by their initials, they were known as the Alpha and Omega of landscape painters. His father Hermann was a merchant who worked in a number of professions, and in 1816 he became manager of a metal factory in Mannheim. Two years later the family moved to Saint Petersburg, where his father wanted to set up a factory.

Edward Poynter served as President of the Royal Academy. He was born in Paris, the son of the architect Ambrose Poynter, though his parents returned to Britain soon after his birth. He was educated at Brighton College and Ipswich School but left school early because of ill health, spending winters in Madeira and Rome. In 1853 he met Frederick Leighton in Rome, who made a great impression on the seventeen-year-old. Back in London he studied at Leigh's Academy in Newman Street.

Cornelis Schut specialised in religious and mythological scenes. He is presumed to have trained under Rubens, and he treated Counter-Reformation subjects in a High-Baroque style. After a stay in Italy, he worked mainly in Antwerp, where he was one of the leading history painters in the first half of the 17th century. He was born in Antwerp, the son of Willem Schut and Suzanna Schernilla. There are no records about his artistic training.

Rafael Barradas absorbed an interest in art from his father at an early age and was almost entirely self-taught. His parents were immigrants from Spain, and his older sister Carmen was a pianist and composer. His younger brother Antonio was a poet. Magazine illustrations were his first professional work, and in 1912 he had his first exhibition, together with Guillermo Laborde. In 1913 a friend invited him to travel to Europe. He was a Uruguayan modernist painter and graphic artist who worked in Spain.

Gesina ter Borch made watercolours and drawings, mostly in albums, that captured her observations of family life, current events and fashionable people. She also wrote love poetry. She was born in Deventer in 1631 and baptised Geesien. She was the first child of the third marriage of Gerard ter Borch the Elder, who taught her to draw and paint. Her father was a draftsman and artist who became a customs collector.

Jean Siméon Chardin is considered a master of still life and is also noted for genre paintings that show kitchen maids, children and domestic activities. Carefully balanced composition, soft diffusion of light and granular impasto characterize his work. He was born in Paris, the son of a cabinetmaker, and rarely left the city. He lived on the Left Bank near Saint-Sulpice until 1757, when Louis XV granted him a studio and living quarters in the Louvre Palace. In 1723 he entered a marriage contract with Marguerite Saintard.
